newsitem.title: USA: Exporter sentenced to jail for defrauding U.S. program.
newsitem.headline: Exporter sentenced to jail for defrauding U.S. program.

text.p: The president of two Florida-based export companies was sentenced to six months in federal prison and fined more than a million dollars on Wednesday for defrauding the Agriculture Department of more than a million dollars worth of payments in dairy export contracts.

U.S. Attorney Eric Holder announced that Harjit Singh of Ft. Lauderdale, Fla., was ordered to pay $1,018,675 in criminal restitution and was given a sentence of six months in federal prison and six months in home detention for making illegal transactions under the government's Diary Export Incentive Programme, otherwise known as DEIP.

Singh is the president of Milk Maid Inc., and MMI International Corp. -- export companies that have won a number of dairy export contracts from the Agriculture Department in the past. Singh and his companies have been suspended from participating in any government contracting programme.

The dairy export programme promotes the sale of U.S. dairy products in foreign countries where the U.S. government has determined it is in the government's interest to expand export markets. The government promotes these sales by making subsidy payments to encourage exporters to sell dairy products in these targeted countries.

Between June 28, 1993 and December 23, 1993, the Justice Department said Singh won eight separate contracts to sell dry milk powder to a company named Marhar International Ltd., which he claimed was located in Dubai, one of the approved recipient countries in the dairy export programme.

Federal investigators, however, discovered that Marhar International was really an off-shore company created and controlled solely by Singh and that the sales of the milk powder were really made to a large food manufacturing company in the Philippines. The Philippines is not an approved country under the dairy export programme.

The Justice Department also said Singh submitted a number of fraudulent shipping documents to the Agriculture Department to hide the true destination of the exports, and used foreign bank accounts to hide the proceeds of the sales and to funnel the funds back into the United States.
